step1_summary: Chief complaint: Sudden onset of profuse watery diarrhoea for 3 days.

Symptoms: • Frequency: almost every hour while awake • Consistency: very watery, no blood • Crampy mid-lower abdominal pain, colicky, ~6/10, precedes bowel actions • Associated: nausea and occasional vomiting (worse with milk), subjective fever/feeling hot, mild ↓ urine output • Able to take some solids but stools remain loose.
Onset/duration: Started ~3 days ago (Mon/Tue); still ongoing.
Aggravating factors: Milk induces vomiting; drinking seems to ‘go straight through’.
Alleviating factors: None stated; takes paracetamol for fever/pain.
Past medical history: Denies chronic illnesses; otherwise fit & well.
Medications/allergies: No regular meds; intermittent paracetamol. No known drug allergies.
Family history: Father with stage-III colon cancer; brother currently has similar 5-day diarrhoeal illness.
Social history: 27-year-old male; lives with mother & sister; office worker; social smoker; alcohol socially/binge monthly; often buys takeaway food; no recent travel mentioned.
Vitals/exam: Tele-visit—no objective vitals. Patient feels febrile but temperature not measured. No physical exam findings provided.

V: Ischaemic colitis: Usually presents with sudden pain + bloody diarrhoea; less likely given age & absence of blood.
I: Acute viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus/rotavirus): Very common, abrupt watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever, person-to-person spread (brother affected).
Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Campylobacter, Salmonella, E. coli, Shigella): Similar presentation; often after contaminated food; may have fever and abdominal cramps.
Giardiasis: Watery foul diarrhoea, nausea, lactose intolerance–like symptoms; possible if contaminated water/food.
N: Colorectal malignancy (early-onset): Family history; can cause change in bowel habit, but acute watery diarrhoea less typical.
Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour: Can produce secretory diarrhoea, flushing/‘hot’ feeling.
D: Primary lactose intolerance: Milk triggers vomiting/diarrhoea; usually chronic but can flare after infections.
Other malabsorption (e.g., pancreatic insufficiency, coeliac) causing diarrhoea.
I2: Drug-induced diarrhoea (e.g., antibiotics, laxatives, metformin): Not on such agents.
C: Congenital enzyme defects (e.g., sucrase-isomaltase deficiency): Would be lifelong; not new.
A: Coeliac disease: Immune-mediated; chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea and weight loss.
T: Abdominal trauma with enteric leak: No history of injury.
E: Hyperthyroidism: Can produce frequent stools/diarrhoea and heat intolerance.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common cause of abrupt, profuse watery diarrhoea with mild fever; highly contagious—brother ill; typically self-limited in young adults.
Similar presentation with abdominal cramping and watery stools; possible if recent takeaway food; feverish sensation supports inflammatory pathogen.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Secondary (transient) lactose intolerance after enteric infection
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Milk ingestion precipitates vomiting; enteric infections can cause temporary lactase deficiency, worsening diarrhoea when dairy consumed.
Can give diarrhoea and crampy pain in 20s age group; however usually more chronic, may have blood/mucus and extra-intestinal features.

supporting_evidence: Brother sick with similar illness—suggests infective spread
Nausea/vomiting and subjective fever typical of viral GE
opposing_evidence: Frequency extremely high (hourly); could also fit severe bacterial infection

supporting_evidence: High stool frequency suggests possible secretory/invasive bacterial pathogen
opposing_evidence: Absence of blood or mucus in stool (common with Campylobacter/Shigella)
No reported recent travel or obvious food exposure
Brother ill—still could be common food source but also fits viral spread

supporting_evidence: Watery diarrhoea can be worsened by dairy products
Often occurs after mucosal injury from viral GE
opposing_evidence: Symptoms not limited to dairy ingestion—diarrhoea ongoing even with other foods
Very acute presentation rather than long-standing intolerance
Acute onset rather than chronic relapsing course
No blood, weight loss, or extra-intestinal symptoms
